name: Autosomal Recessive Epidermolytic Ichthyosis

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: Clinical and Histopathological Diagnostic Criteria for Epidermolytic Ichthyosis

criteria.description: Presence of generalized blistering and erythroderma at birth or neonatal period
Skin biopsy showing epidermolytic hyperkeratosis with vacuolar degeneration of the upper epidermis
Identification of biallelic pathogenic variants in KRT10 or KRT1 genes consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance
Consanguinity or affected siblings supporting autosomal recessive inheritance

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: All three major criteria (clinical presentation, histopathology, and genetic testing) must be met for definitive diagnosis.
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Differentiation from autosomal dominant epidermolytic ichthyosis is critical due to inheritance pattern and genetic counseling implications.

pathognomonic.notes: Blistering typically involves widespread skin areas and is present in the neonatal period.

pathognomonic.symptomName: Epidermolytic hyperkeratosis with thickened, scaly skin plaques
pathognomonic.notes: Hyperkeratosis develops progressively after initial blistering phase.
Redness and inflammation of the skin often accompany blistering.
searchTerms: red skin covering whole body at birth

common.notes: Thickening of skin on palms and soles is frequently observed.
Flexural involvement is common with thickened skin folds.
Itching is a frequent symptom causing discomfort.
Due to skin barrier disruption, bacterial infections are common.
Abnormal nail growth or structure may be present.

occasional.notes: Hair involvement can occur but is less frequent.
searchTerms: hair loss or abnormal hair texture

occasional.notes: Increased sweating of palms and soles may be noted.
searchTerms: excessive sweating on palms and soles
increased sweat in hands and feet

occasional.notes: Eyelid eversion can occur secondary to skin tightness.
Due to impaired sweating and skin barrier.
Limited joint mobility may develop from skin tightening.

rare.symptomName: Severe bacterial sepsis secondary to skin barrier disruption
rare.notes: Life-threatening infections can rarely occur in neonates.
searchTerms: severe bacterial infection from skin barrier loss
bacterial sepsis due to skin damage

rare.symptomName: Electrolyte imbalance due to extensive skin loss
rare.notes: Rarely seen in severe neonatal cases with widespread blistering.
searchTerms: electrolyte problems due to skin shedding
fluid and electrolyte loss from skin damage
corneal ulcers from eyelid turning out
eye surface sores due to ectropion

laboratory: Skin biopsy showing epidermolytic hyperkeratosis with vacuolar degeneration
Elevated inflammatory markers during secondary infections
imaging: Not routinely required; imaging may be used to assess joint contractures if present
genetic: Biallelic pathogenic variants in KRT10 or KRT1 genes confirming autosomal recessive inheritance
other: Family history consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance or consanguinity

distinguishingFeatures: Heterozygous mutations in KRT1 or KRT10

redFlags: Severe generalized blistering and erythroderma in neonate
Rapid development of secondary bacterial infections
Signs of systemic infection or sepsis
references: Orphanet: Autosomal recessive epidermolytic ichthyosis - ORPHA:512103
Fischer J, et al. Epidermolytic ichthyosis: clinical, histopathological, and molecular aspects. J Am Acad Dermatol. 2013.
